daysW1.title: Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port -> Orisson
daysW1.short_desc: Wet Start to a Grand Adventure, El Camino Francés
daysW1.long_desc: Rain when we left Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port behind toward the Pyrenees and El Camino Francés. Started with an 800 meter climb, more mountain trekking than walking, toward Orisson hostel, nestled in the mountains like a small oasis.That evening, we gathered for a traditional pilgrims dinner with warm food, red wine and laughter with fellow travelers from all corners of the world, each with their own story. Hang tight,pictures are on the way. Just dealing with a slow internet connection.

daysW1.title: Orisson -> Roncesvalles
daysW1.short_desc: Crossing the Pyrenees toward the Monastery in Roncesvalles.
daysW1.long_desc: After breakfast at the Orisson hostel, we set off around eight o’clock, ready to cross the Pyrenees toward today’s destination Roncesvalles. Half way, just before the trail turns off the road and out onto the open moorland, stood the day’s savior, a Food truck. Steaming hot chocolate and a simple sandwich tasted like a luxury brunch with a mountain view, an invaluable break. But that’s exactly where it’s easy to go wrong, especially in fog. Two Australian women from Alice Springs and Darwin learned that the hard way the day before. In heavy fog and rain, they missed the sign and continued straight ahead. Four kilometers later, they realized their mistake, wandered around for a while, and were eventually picked up by a kind driver who brought them back to Orisson. There, food and extra beds were waiting, something the hostel wisely keeps on hand for just such occasions. Today’s weather, however, was perfect for hiking,  clear skies, good visibility and not a drop of rain. The Pyrenees showed their best side, freely roaming sheep and cattle, horses grazing across the open fields, and a view so breathtaking it almost demanded poetry. This make the Camino so alive and so unique.

daysW1.title: Roncesvalles -> Zubiri
daysW1.short_desc: Hostel Suseia deserves the highest praise, and then some.
daysW1.long_desc: The rain returned after lunch and combined with steep hills, muddy trails and treacherous rocks, the trail turned into a true challenge. The terrain was demanding and the footing deceptively tricky, with a few minor falls serving as reminders that El Camino Francés demands respect, patience, and understanding. But after many meters of elevation and tough trials, we finally reached Zubiri and Hostel Suseia, a true gem along the trail, where the hostess and owner Sara welcomed us as old friends. This wasn’t just a place to stay, it was an fantastic experience. With an incredible sense of hospitality, a warm and welcoming atmosphere, and authentic Spanish food and drink traditions of the highest class. The evening became magical and unforgettable. For us 11 pilgrims from different corners of the world, it was a night of togetherness, laughter, and delicious food.

daysW1.title: Zubiri -> Pamplona
daysW1.short_desc: The Road to Pamplona and Tapas with Hemingway.
daysW1.long_desc: We left Zubiri around nine o’clock, a bit later than planned, but with light steps and perfect hiking weather. Today’s goal was the historic city of Pamplona, our first milestone on El Camino Francés. The path was far from flat. It wound up and down through the beautiful Basque countryside, with small villages appearing like little oases along the trail. After about 12 kilometers, we reached Irotz, home to a popular lunch stop offering food, drinks and some much needed rest. Refueled and refreshed, we pushed on toward Pamplona. By the time we reached the city Arre, the fatigue was creeping in and we found ourselves wishing we had booked a place to stay there. From Arre, it’s still 5 tough kilometers to the heart of Pamplona and you feel every one of them. But all weariness was quickly forgotten upon arrival. Pamplona is a vibrant city full of history, tradition, celebration and energy. In the evening, we treated ourselves to tapas at the legendary Café Iruña, the favorite spot of none other than Ernest Hemingway himself. And as if the day weren’t already perfect, we bumped into our Bed Bunker Buddies, Amelia and Ed from Virginia, whom we had met earlier on the trail. The reunion was celebrated with laughter, wine and that unmistakable Camino spirit.

daysW1.title: 27 kilometers, countless climbs, sweat and our Camino’s longest day so far.
daysW1.short_desc: 27 km, countless climbs, sweat, and our Camino’s longest day so far!
daysW1.long_desc: We knew it was going to be a long day, so by 8:00 AM we had already left Pamplona behind, with Puente la Reina set as our destination. 27 kilometers lay ahead, our longest stage on the Camino so far. Just outside the city, we made a quick stop at Colegio Mayor Belagua, where we had our pilgrim passports, Compostela, stamped. Then came the real challenge, the climb up to Alto de Perdón, the iconic ridge where iron sculptures of pilgrims stand facing the wind and the horizon. It’s a magical place, but a brutal one to reach, with steep elevation and legs full of lactic acid. And the view from the top? Worth every single step. Eventually, we arrived at Albergue Estrella Guia, a hostel only for pilgrims, where we were welcomed not by the sun, but by the warm, spiritual energy of our host, Natalia. She greeted us like family, with care, joy, and the comforting feeling of being truly home for the night. The day ended with dinner at the lovely, highly recommended local restaurant Venta de Vino, Ganbara, Artesania. Great food and vine, good and the strong sense that we are now fully immersed in the daily rhythm of the Camino.  .
